description: Signs of Arjuna's despondency (viṣāda) on seeing his kin arrayed for battle, in his own words: his limbs give way, his mouth dries, his body trembles, his hair stands on end, the bow Gāṇḍīva slips from his hand, his skin burns, he cannot stand steady and his mind seems to whirl (1.28–30). The adverse omens he sees (1.31) are recorded separately (phn:bhagavad-gita-adverse-omens).
What is night for all beings, the self-controlled one is awake in; what beings are awake in is night for the seeing sage.
Arjuna sees adverse omens (nimittāni viparītāni) and foresees no good in killing his kin.
The brāhmī sthiti: having attained it one is no longer deluded; abiding in it even at death one attains brahmanirvāṇa.

When understanding crosses the thicket of delusion one becomes indifferent to what is to be heard and what has been heard; when understanding, perplexed by what it has heard, stands unmoving and immovable in samādhi, one attains yoga.
Knowledge is covered by desire as fire by smoke, a mirror by dirt (mala), an embryo by its membrane; desire, seated in the senses, mind and understanding, deludes the embodied one.
Desires enter the one who attains peace as waters enter the ocean, which is ever filled yet stands unmoved.
Serenity (prasāda): attained by one who moves among objects with senses free of attraction and aversion; in it all sorrows cease and the understanding quickly becomes steady.

stage: one who has seen the highest
description: When one abstains from sense-objects they turn away but the taste (rasa) for them remains; even the taste turns away when one has seen the highest (param).
Even for a discerning person who strives, the turbulent senses forcibly carry away the mind, and the mind following them carries away wisdom as wind a ship.

Marks of the one of steady wisdom: all desires given up, content in the self by the self; unshaken by sorrow, without craving in pleasure, free from passion, fear and anger; neither rejoicing nor hating; senses withdrawn like a tortoise's limbs; awake in what is night for all beings and seeing as night what beings wake to; filled by desires as the ocean by waters yet unmoved; without 'mine' and 'I'; at peace; not bewildered; abiding in this brahmic state even at death.
